newsitem.title: NIGERIA: Banks keen to tap Nigerian oil fund money.
newsitem.headline: Banks keen to tap Nigerian oil fund money.

text.p: Nigerian banks are keen to tap the pool of cash building up in a special fund set up by the military government to cushion the economy from higher fuel prices.

"Banks are keen to get the money, but only if it is offered at a very good price," one banker said. "Last time the banks snapped up the money, and then found there was nothing to do with it because nobody wanted to borrow with the economy so lifeless."
Officials of the government's Petroleum Trust Fund (PTF) said bankers were meeting with the managers of the fund in the capital Abuja on Tuesday.
"I believe the meeting is not unconnected with the next disbursement of funds," PTF spokesman Yau Darazo told Reuters.
Darazao said he did not know the amount in question. But the newspaper Thisday speculated on Monday there could be as much as 15 billion naira ($190 million) available in the latest release of funds.
The PTF was set up in October 1994, after a four-fold rise in fuel prices, with the aim of recycling the extra tax revenue into projects to develop the overall economy.
The fund has so far not made public the details of what it has earned or exactly what it has spent. PTF money stays with the banks only until it is paid to contractors.
Analysts' estimates of the total amount which has flowed into the fund since 1994 vary from 40 billion to 60 billion naira.
The last gush of money from the fund was blamed by some analysts for a jump in May's month-on-month inflation figures, and the central bank said it had to take moves to mop up excess liquidity.

The PTF says it could not sabotage Nigeria's tight fiscal policy, aimed at keeping inflation under control. "It is not new money, it is money that was spent at the fuel pumps, that was already circulating in the system, any effect on inflation can only be negligible," Darazo said.
The PTF gets 5.32 naira from the 11 naira cost of a litre of petrol, compared with a 1.70 naira share for refineries and distribution and 1.30 naira for marketers.
The PTF's clear beneficiaries so far have been construction and pharmaceutical industries.
Contracts worth 32 billion naira have been awarded for road repairs, as well as 1.5 billion naira for the supply of drugs. It is not known what proportion of contracts have been paid.
"Some of our companies have actually increased capacity, others have doubled utilisation from 10 to 20 percent," said Jacob Eno, of the Pharmaceutical Manufacturers Group.
Contracts were shared among 38 drug companies, including BCN, Evans Medical, May & Baker, Pfizer Products and Smithkline Beecham.
The 17 construction companies benefiting from PTF contracts include Julius Berger, Roads Nigeria, Strabag and Impresit Bakolori.
"If the PTF gets it right then by reducing transport costs they will also reduce inflation," said Uzor Okeke, director-general of the Manufacturers Association of Nigeria.
"Unfortunately the impression we have in eastern Nigeria is that contractors are not doing the job," he added.

Accountability is a worry for many analysts in a country with a history of public money going astray -- in spite of the appointment as chairman of retired major-general Mohammed Buhari, a former military ruler with reputation for discipline.
"It seems that everything they have done so far has been sensible, but it would be better if figures were available," World Bank economist Thomas Hutcheson said recently.
The PTF has no deadline to end operations.
($1=79 naira)
